Regional flexibility that allows for intraregional differentiation in cost responsibility can enable more granular cost allocation to users that bear the greatest cost responsibility or receive the greatest benefits from the project. The SPP and MISO tariffs illustrate two approaches to subregional cost allocation. 23 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. SPP’s Highway/Byway method uses a voltage threshold to determine the distribution of project costs among local and regional ratepayers. The underlying philosophy is lower- voltage projects primarily benefit local network users, whereas higher-voltage projects have regional benefits. The MISO footprint consists of a diverse mix of states divided into two subregions, MISO Midwest and MISO South. Although the case study took place before MISO South was added, subsequent MISO MVP tranches allow costs to be allocated to one or both subregions based on the benefits the projects provide. Subregional cost allocation can enable MISO to focus cost responsibility on the subregion driving the transmission need and receiving the most. The regional flexibility also allows MISO to use different cost allocations for other types of transmission projects. Regional flexibility enables more granular cost allocation without introducing a complex method based on power system modeling. In both MISO and SPP, the actual cost allocation of the regionally-allocated project is based on a simple load ratio share. Power system models are used prior to cost allocation to evaluate project benefits in MISO and to validate the Highway/Byway method in SPP but are not part of the cost allocation calculation. In addition, both MISO and SPP evaluate and quantify a broad range of benefit types, which has the added advantage of producing a set of benefits that is more evenly distributed and more stable over time than any single metric–thereby facilitating cost allocation. In contrast, when only individual metrics are used, such as power flows in PJM, the resulting uneven distribution of benefits can more readily lead to disputes. 3. A backstop or default cost allocation method allows flexibility for project-specific cost allocation agreements while also ensuring selected projects can move forward if an alternative agreement is not reached. The NYISO’s PPTPP and SPP-MISO JTIQ projects illustrate the application of a backstop method to reduce the risk of projects stalling as a result of disputes about cost allocation methods. For public policy projects in the NYISO, the NYPSC can recommend an alternative cost allocation method tailored to the characteristics of the project. For the NYISO’s AC Transmission Needs projects, the NYPSC identified an alternative cost allocation method that assigns more cost responsibility to the zones that receive economic benefits from the project.
